sessions.teaching:
The passage many churches read every time they take communion, the warning to examine yourself so you don't eat and drink judgment, has often been pulled so far from its setting that it produces nearly the opposite of what Paul intended. In many churches it produces a room of anxious individuals, heads bowed, each searching their own heart for some hidden sin that might make the bread dangerous. Paul wrote those words in anger at a church that was humiliating its poor members at the very meal meant to make them one. So we need to read the chapter the way he wrote it. The misreading isn't harmless. It turns a rebuke of division into a summons to introspection, and it lets a church commit the sin Paul condemned while feeling solemn about it.

Here's what seems to have been happening. The Lord's Supper in the early church was part of a real meal, usually in the home of one of the better-off members. Paul writes, "In eating, each one goes ahead with his own meal. One goes hungry, another gets drunk" (1 Corinthians 11:21). Many scholars think the wealthier members, who had leisure, arrived early and ate and drank their fill, while laborers and slaves who couldn't leave work until later arrived to find little or nothing left. Paul's rebuke is sharp: "Do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing?" (1 Corinthians 11:22). The meal that proclaimed a Lord who emptied himself for the lowly had become a weekly display of the very divisions the gospel abolishes.

That, Paul says, is why they eat and drink judgment: "For anyone who eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment on himself" (1 Corinthians 11:29). Hold on to that phrase, "the body," because everything turns on it. Many of us have heard it as a command to reverence the bread. But Paul has just written, "Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread" (1 Corinthians 10:17), and in the next chapter he develops the church as a body whose members, Jews and Greeks, slaves and free, all belong (1 Corinthians 12:12-13). The body they were failing to discern was not only the bread. It was one another. They had learned to take the table without looking at how they treated the people beside them.

The introspective reading has truth in it, and I don't want to overcorrect. Self-examination is biblical. "Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup" (1 Corinthians 11:28). A casual, careless approach to holy things is a real danger. Reverence matters. But the examination Paul commands here starts by looking outward before it looks inward. Before it sends you to hunt for private sin, it asks how you're treating your brothers and sisters, and whether the way you come to the table honors or humiliates the body of Christ. Jesus gives the same order: "First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift" (Matthew 5:24). Paul's practical instruction at the end is almost plain: "So then, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another" (1 Corinthians 11:33).

I stand inside this with everyone else. We've taken the one meal that proclaims a death that reconciles enemies, that breaks down "the dividing wall of hostility" (Ephesians 2:14), and too often made it a quiet marker of who's respectable enough to belong. Many of us have passed the bread to someone we were cold toward and called it communion. Pastors have led the table while carrying a division in their own hearts that the meal in their hands was preaching against.

Paul says that "as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes" (1 Corinthians 11:26). The table is a sermon preached with the body. A church that eats it while despising part of its own body proclaims a reconciliation it refuses to live. So the examination the table asks for isn't mainly the anxious search for private failure that has made so many Christians afraid of the bread. It's the harder, humbler question of whether you're at peace with the body you're about to eat with, whether there's someone to be reconciled to first, whether a division you've made your peace with is being carried right up to the table of the Lord who died to end it.

The meal was given to make us one. It still can. And it still judges the church that won't let it. Come to it, then, not only to search your own heart alone, but to be made one with the body of Christ. Where you can't come in peace with a brother, go and be reconciled first. Then come, eat, and proclaim with your body a death that brings enemies home.

scriptureStudy.note: "When you come together as a church, I hear that there are divisions among you." Paul names the problem at the start, and it's division.
"One goes hungry, another gets drunk... Do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing?" The specific sin is the comfortable shaming the poor at the meal.
"Anyone who eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment on himself." In context, discerning the body includes recognizing the church, not only reverencing the bread.
"Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread." The one loaf is itself an argument for unity.
"For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body," Jews and Greeks, slaves and free. Paul's picture of the church as one body stands behind chapter 11.
"First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift." Jesus puts reconciliation before worship, the same order Paul presses at the table.
"For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility." The cross the table proclaims is the death that reconciles enemies.

sessions.goingDeeper:
The social world of Corinth explains the abuse and sharpens the warning. Gordon Fee, in his commentary on 1 Corinthians (1987), draws on studies of Roman houses to suggest that the Supper was joined to a meal in a wealthier member's home, where the dining room held only a few guests and the rest gathered in a larger courtyard. If so, the architecture itself reinforced the ranking the gospel abolished: the honored few reclining with the host, the many outside. Roman society was ordered by patronage and rank to a degree modern readers struggle to feel, and reproducing that order at the table of a crucified Lord wasn't a small lapse.

A group might ask how often the church still sorts people by money, status, and respectability and carries that sorting into the room where we proclaim that Christ died for all of them. If the table is a sermon preached with the body, then the unity or division of the church at the table is part of what it preaches. Let the table examine the church the way Paul meant it to, and let it send people not only to a private mirror but to a brother.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a sincere, diligent member of your group has quietly stopped taking communion for months. When the session reaches "examine yourself," she admits with real distress that she never feels worthy enough, that she's always sure some sin hasn't been adequately confessed, and that the warning about judgment has made the table a source of dread.

She isn't being dramatic. She's been handed a misreading, and it has wounded a tender conscience. Don't simply tell her worthiness doesn't matter; Paul does say to examine yourself, and a quick reassurance would ring false. Give her the passage back whole. The "unworthy manner" Paul condemns was the comfortable humiliating the poor, not a tender conscience with doubts. The worthiness he asks for isn't moral perfection. It's coming as a sinner to a gracious host, discerning and loving the body rather than despising it. A heart afraid it isn't good enough is exactly the heart this table was spread for. Send her back to the bread, not away from it.

leaderPrimer:
The particular danger of a study on baptism and communion is that it turns into a debate club. You're handling the two subjects the church has argued over longest, and if you let it, the room will split into teams and spend five weeks scoring points: Baptist against Presbyterian, memorial view against real presence, everyone defending the tradition they grew up in and no one being formed. So set one rule the first night and keep it every night after. The goal isn't to win. It's to understand what these signs are, to hold real convictions with real humility, and to state the view you disagree with so well that its own defenders would sign your summary. Ask people to state the view they don't hold, in its strongest form, before they critique it. That one habit will do more for the room than any lecture.

Be clear, and say it more than once, about the difference between what the faith stands or falls on and what faithful churches disagree on and remain one. The deity and resurrection of Christ and salvation by grace through the cross are first-order and not up for a vote. Who should be baptized and how Christ is present at the Supper are second-order: worth studying, deciding, and holding, and never worth breaking fellowship over. I say plainly where I land, and I work to state the other views at their strongest. Do the same, whatever your own tradition. If your group comes from one tradition, work extra hard to represent the others fairly. If it's mixed, keep the temperature low and the depth high.

Watch for two kinds of people. One is the new believer who has never been baptized or never understood the table. For them this study is an invitation, not a debate, so don't let the arguing drown out the wonder. The other is the person with a wounded conscience, especially around the "examine yourself" passage, who has been made afraid of the table and needs the passage given back whole rather than another warning. Lead as someone still being taught by the water and the meal, and the room will follow you into honesty instead of into teams.

faq.q: Is this study going to tell me my baptism was wrong, or that my church has communion wrong?
faq.a: No. The method is to state each position on baptism and on the Lord's Supper in the form its own best defenders would recognize before any verdict. I say where I land, and I still try to make the infant-baptism case and the range of communion views as strong as their advocates would want. The aim is to help you understand what these signs are, hold your convictions with more depth and humility, and see that these are questions on which faithful churches have disagreed for centuries while remaining one body.

faq.q: Why does the study call baptism and communion second-order issues? Don't they matter?
faq.a: They matter a great deal, which is why the study gives them five sessions. Second-order doesn't mean unimportant. It means they aren't the doctrines the faith stands or falls on, the way the deity and bodily resurrection of Christ and salvation by grace through the cross are. Baptism and the Supper are worth deciding and holding with conviction. They aren't worth breaking fellowship over, because faithful churches have landed on opposite sides while confessing the same Lord.

faq.q: What's the difference between a sacrament and an ordinance?
faq.a: The words mark a real difference in emphasis. The Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, and Reformed churches say sacrament and mean that God actually gives grace through the sign. Many Baptist and free churches say ordinance, meaning a practice Christ commanded, an act of obedience and public proclamation, and they're careful not to locate any saving power in the water or the bread. The ordinance instinct guards the truth that no one is saved by getting wet or eating. The sacrament instinct guards the truth that God is generous enough to meet us in ordinary created things. The study treats the difference as one among brothers and sisters.

faq.q: Does the study say what happens at communion, or does it dodge the question?
faq.a: It doesn't dodge it. Session four sets out four views at their strongest: the memorial view associated with Zwingli, the spiritual-presence view associated with Calvin, the Lutheran view, and transubstantiation as the Roman Catholic Church defines it. It names what each one guards. Then I say where I land: closest to Calvin, confessing that the living Christ is really present by his Spirit to feed his people. I hold it as a second-order conviction and say plainly that the real tragedy is turning a meal of grace into a border checkpoint.

faq.q: I'm not sure I believe any of this. Can a skeptic get anything out of the study?
faq.a: Yes. It begins by taking seriously the instinct you may bring with you: that the real world is what you can measure and that religious rituals look like leftover superstition. I came to faith from atheism, so I don't pretend that instinct away. The study explains why Christianity, unlike a philosophy, refuses to stay in the head and insists on things you can touch, and how that's rooted in a God who made a material world, called it good, and took on a body himself. You don't have to share the conclusion to find the reasoning worth following.

faq.q: Why spend a whole session on Romans 6 instead of just explaining baptism?
faq.a: Because the argument over who gets baptized can distract from what baptism declares, which both traditions confess together. Session three stands where every tradition stands: baptism as burial and resurrection with Christ. It speaks directly to anyone weighed down by shame or defined by an old failure. It distinguishes a change of standing, which is complete in Christ, from a change of condition, which takes a lifetime, and shows that the Christian life is learning to live from a newness already given.

faq.q: Will the study make me anxious about taking communion the wrong way?
faq.a: It aims to do the opposite. The "examine yourself" passage has often been read as a call to search for hidden sin. Paul wrote it to rebuke a church where the comfortable ate their fill while the poor went hungry at the meal meant to make them one. The examination he asks for starts with how we treat our brothers and sisters. The study gives the passage back whole, and it takes special care with anyone who has stayed away from the table out of fear.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I'm not a theologian and don't know all the views?
faq.a: That's who the study was written for. Each session carries the teaching in full, states each contested view at its strongest, and puts a note behind every question. Your job isn't to be the expert. It's to keep the room fair and humble, ask people to state the view they disagree with well before they critique it, and hold the line between first-order and second-order matters. Read the primer, read the teaching before your group meets, and lead as someone learning alongside the room.

faq.q: My group is all from one tradition. Is the study still worth doing?
faq.a: Yes, and the discipline may matter more. A room that only ever hears other views caricatured will leave more tribal than it came. The study asks you to state the views you don't hold in their strongest form, which is exactly the muscle a single-tradition group tends not to build. If anything, the leader should feel free to argue the other side well so no one leaves thinking those who disagree are careless with the Bible.

faq.q: Doesn't taking a clear position contradict the call to be charitable?
faq.a: No. Charity doesn't mean having no convictions or pretending every view is equally right. It means holding convictions with courage and love, stating the other side fairly, and refusing to make a second-order disagreement a test of fellowship. I say where I land on both baptism and the Supper, name the strongest objections I haven't fully answered, and treat those who disagree as brothers and sisters. Conviction and humility belong in the same hand.

faq.q: What if someone in the group has never been baptized or never understood communion?
faq.a: That's one of the best reasons to do the study, and the leader should make sure the arguing never drowns out the invitation. Session one recovers why the signs matter, session two calls the unbaptized believer to the sign at the door, session three shows what baptism says about who they are, and sessions four and five open the table as a meal of grace. If someone professes faith in Christ and has never been baptized, take it seriously and connect them with your pastor.

timeline.event: On the night he is betrayed, Jesus takes bread and the cup with his disciples and gives them the meal. After his resurrection he commands his church to make disciples and baptize them.
At Pentecost Peter preaches "repent and be baptized," and about three thousand are baptized (Acts 2:38-41).
Paul writes 1 Corinthians, the earliest written account of the Lord's Supper we have, rebuking a church that shamed its poor at the table.

timeline.date: Late first or early second century
timeline.event: The Didache, an early church manual, gives instructions for baptism and for the thanksgiving meal.
Justin Martyr, writing to the emperor, describes the baptism of new believers and the weekly gathering where bread and a cup are shared.
Irenaeus of Lyon, in Against Heresies, answers teachers who despised the material world, pointing to the Supper as proof that God redeems what he made.
Cyprian and a council of North African bishops debate not whether to baptize infants but whether to wait until the eighth day, and decide they need not.
Augustine describes a sacrament as the word joined to an element, "a kind of visible word," and defends infant baptism against the Pelagians.
The Fourth Lateran Council uses the language of transubstantiation for the change of the bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ.
In Zurich, a small group baptizes one another as believers against the state church, beginning the movement later called Anabaptist. Zwingli teaches a memorial understanding of the Supper.
At the Marburg Colloquy, Luther and Zwingli fail to agree on the presence of Christ in the Supper.
John Calvin publishes the first edition of his Institutes, later developing an account of the Supper in which believers truly feed on Christ by the Holy Spirit.
The Council of Trent defines transubstantiation against the Reformers.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thanks for being here. We're taking up the two subjects the church has argued about longest, and it takes some courage to do that well. Three things before we start. First, the goal isn't to win. It's to understand what these signs are and to hold our convictions with humility. So here's our rule: before anyone critiques a view they don't hold, they need to be able to state it in its strongest form. Second, we'll keep a clear line between what the faith stands or falls on, which isn't up for debate here, and what faithful churches disagree on and remain one, which is most of what we'll discuss. You can disagree with the person next to you about baptism or the table and still be brothers and sisters, and we'll act like it. Third, if you've never been baptized, or you've been made afraid of the communion table, this study is an invitation to you, not a debate to survive, and I'm glad to talk privately anytime. Tonight we're looking at ________. Let me read our passage, and we'll sit with it a moment before anyone speaks.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked at what the passage says. Now let's bring it home, off the map of positions and into how each of us actually comes to the water and the table, because none of this matters if it never touches the way we receive them ourselves.
facilitatorScript.close: We'll stop here, even though it isn't all resolved. The church has held some of these questions in tension for a very long time, and we won't settle them in an evening. Try the practice this week, and sit with the reflection questions on your own. If tonight raised a question about your own baptism or your place at the table, don't carry it alone; come find me. Let me pray for us before we go. And thank you for holding these things without turning into teams. That's harder than winning, and better.

glossary.definition: In the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, and Reformed traditions, a sign given by Christ through which God gives grace. Augustine described it as the word joined to an element, "a kind of visible word."
In many Baptist and free-church traditions, a practice Christ commanded, an act of obedience and public proclamation, with care not to locate saving power in the water or bread.
A way God gives grace to his people, such as the preached word, prayer, and, in the sacramental traditions, baptism and the Supper.
Believer's baptism, the conviction that baptism belongs to those who can profess faith. The view I hold, as a second-order conviction.
Infant baptism, the conviction that the covenant sign belongs on the children of believers, as circumcision did in Israel.
The argument that Scripture is one covenant of grace across both Testaments, so the sign moves from circumcision to baptism while its recipients, believers and their children, stay the same.
The teaching of Romans 6 that the believer is so joined to Christ that his death and resurrection count as theirs.
Associated with Zwingli, the view that "this is my body" means "this represents my body," and the Supper is an act of remembrance.
Associated with Calvin, the view that Christ is truly present at the table to faith, and by the Spirit believers feed on him. The view I land closest to.

The Lutheran view that Christ's body and blood are truly present "in, with, and under" the bread and wine while the bread remains bread. Sometimes called consubstantiation, a term Lutherans generally reject.

The Roman Catholic teaching, stated at the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) and defined at Trent (1551), that the substance of the bread and wine becomes Christ's body and blood while the appearances remain.
The broad conviction, shared in different forms by Lutheran, Roman Catholic, and Reformed churches, that Christ is truly present at the table and not only remembered.
Paul's phrase in 1 Corinthians 11:29, which in context includes recognizing the church as one body, not only reverencing the bread.
A matter worth deciding and holding with conviction, on which faithful churches disagree while remaining one in the faith.
